newsitem.title: Tanzania: Rwandan refugees hide in Tanzania bush.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees hide in Tanzania bush.

text.p: Rwandan refugees in Tanzania hid in the bush on Tuesday to avoid repatriation but U.N. refugee agency officials differed on the number who fled their camps.

Aid workers meanwhile said they believed Tanzanian troop reinforcements were heading for the camps area in the northwest to push the government campaign for the 542,000 Rwandan refugees to go home by December 31.

"We hear large numbers of Tanzanian military are heading this way and the authorities have warned those who have escaped from the camps they face arrest," said one aid worker, who declined to be identified.
"It seems there will be some action this weekend," he added in Ngara, the centre for relief agencies working in the 13 camps in the northwest.
There was no official Tanzanian confirmation that more troops were being deployed to the area.
The U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) said earlier on Tuesday about 23,000 refugees fled into the bush after last week's order to return to the homeland they left in 1994.
Peter Kessler, a UNHCR spokesman in Nairobi, lowered the figure later.

"After a tour of the camps we now think the maximum number who fled were 15,000, of which several thousand have come back. We now think only some 10,000 remain in the bush. Most of them fled on Sunday," Kessler said.
But UNHCR officials in Ngara said they stood by the 23,000 figure.
A larger group of 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire was displaced by fighting that began in mid-October. More than 500,000 returned in November while the others fled north and west.
Senior Tanzanian officials visited the UNHCR regional headquarters in Ngara on Tuesday but U.N. officials declined to say what was discussed.
Tanzania said last week its army would take part in the repatriation operation if necessary but has not said what will happen to those who refuse to return voluntarily.
Kessler said a total of 1,928 Rwandan refugees voluntarily left Tanzania camps on Tuesday and were trucked back to Rwanda.
"That is the biggest figure in a very long time and it brings to more than 3,500 the total this month who returned," he said.
UNHCR officials said the Interahamwe, Rwandan Hutu militiamen who led the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, had intensified intimidation of refugees.

The Interahamwe are determined not to go home as they fear reprisals for their role in the slaughter of up to one million Tutsis and Hutu moderates in Rwanda in 1994. They fled when Tutsi rebels took power in Rwanda.
Some of the refugees in Tanzania say they are willing to go back in large groups but many others say they do not trust Rwanda's new government.
The repatriation plan has been attacked by the London-based human rights group Amnesty International and exiled Hutu lobby group Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy in Rwanda.
The two groups accuse UNHCR of abandoning its principle of protecting refugees against forced repatriation.
